title: How to read a calibration curve without fooling yourself
intro: A short, practical guide to the four checks that catch most calibration mistakes before they reach a dataset.

add_content_to_page.add_paragraph: A calibration curve is a claim about the relationship between what an instrument reports and what is actually there. Most of the failures we see are not statistical — they are procedural, and they show up in the shape of the residuals.

add_special_note.heading: Before you fit anything
add_special_note.text: Plot the raw points. If the calibration standards were prepared in the wrong order, no fitting method will rescue them.

add_items_to_list: Run at least three blanks, not one.
A blank that drifts upward across the run usually means carry-over.
Subtract the blank mean, not the first blank.

add_heading.heading_text: 2. Look at the residuals, not R²

add_content_to_page.add_paragraph: A high R² can hide a curve that is systematically wrong at the low end. Plot residual against concentration; a smile or a frown means the model is the wrong shape.

add_equation.heading: The linear model you are checking

add_content_to_page.add_paragraph: Prepare a standard your calibration does not include and predict it. That single number is worth more than any goodness-of-fit statistic.
Temperature, humidity and the age of the standards belong beside the curve. When a series drifts three weeks later, these are the variables you will wish you had.
